Actual versus Aspirational Student Growth

It seems simple enough: Establish what constitutes a year’s growth
in a year’s time for each student.
This simplicity belies a subtle complexity.
To adequately address the notion of a year’s growth, actual growth
must be distinguished from aspirational growth.
Describe What is a current year’s growth?
Prescribe What should a current year’s growth be?
Answering the second question establishes a threshold
distinguishing adequate from inadequate growth.
To make such a distinction requires an answer to the first question
which defines a norm: What is the range of growth currently
observed?
Aspirational growth should be possible—This is Linn’s existence
proof applied at the individual level [Linn, 2003].

Describing Actual Student Growth

Measuring student growth, even with a vertical scale, is not a simple
task.
Numerous States believe that placing their tests on a vertical scale
will simplify the task of measuring student growth.
Even with an interval (or ratio) scale, growth is not easy to interpret.
Consider, for example, height.
A child might grow 4 inches between ages 3 and 4.
4 inches is a well understood quantity.
However, the 4 inch increase becomes fully understandable only when
placed in context of growth of similar children.
In the following discussion student growth percentiles are introduced
that provide a normative context in which to interpret student growth.

Student Growth Percentiles
As the figures indicate, there is a distribution of 2006 scale scores
associated with each 2005 scale score.
The average (or median) of the conditional density could be used as
a point estimate of the 2006 scale score given the student’s 2005
performance.
This point estimate could be used to define “expected”, “average”, or
“typical” growth.
Similarly, the middle 50% of each density gives a range of scores
where one would expect such a student’s score to reside 50% of the
time.
Using quantile regression techniques, conditional densities using
more than a single prior score can be estimated.
Given a student’s prior scale scores and the associated conditional
density, their current scale score corresponds to a percentile of that
conditional distribution.
This percentile is the student’s growth percentile.
For example, a student growth percentile of 60 indicates the student’s
latest scale score exceeded 60 percent of his/her counterparts with
equal prior scores.

Student Growth Percentiles
Student growth percentiles norm each student’s progress relative to
similarly performing students.
The growth percentiles are estimated using quantile regression
techniques (Betebenner & Shang, 2007; Koenker, 2005).
The percentile scale on which the growth percentiles lie allows for
easy comparison of all students.
For example, consider a low achieving student demonstrating 90th
percentile growth and a high achieving student demonstrating 10th
percentile growth.
The low achieving student grew at a rate exceeding 90 percent of their
academic peers.1
The high achieving student grew at a rate exceeding just 10 percent of
their academic peers.
In this sense, the low achiever’s growth is more extraordinary than the
high achiever’s.
Judgment of whether the student’s growth is adequate requires
external criteria specifying adequate for what?.
The term academic peers is used to describe those students with equal prior
achievement.
